Same-session interleaved A/B on scene-default, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1, 3 reps, TREEORDER (pathtracer) vs RANDORDER (scratch/wideA, identical wide build with original triangle order): TREEORDER render_ms_best 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 (gpu_ms_best 45.700 / 46.379 / 46.017) vs RANDORDER 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 (gpu_ms_best 45.731 / 43.924 / 43.585). Decision: revert — the change failed the keep-wins-only rule (it was a loss, not a win), and the cache-locality hypothesis didn't pay off, presumably because shadow/refraction rays hit triangles in a pattern that reordering doesn't align with. The current pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp confirms the revert: its header comment states the payload is the triangle index into TriData 'which keeps the original triangle order' (tool output #281), and the file content I re-read at #289 has no tri_data emission code in BuildWideNode.

What I did: changed the builder so TriData records are appended when a leaf is emitted (depth-first), with the leaf payload holding that new index instead of the original triangle id, so spatially neighbouring leaves index adjacent triangle records (edits at messages #87, #89, #95-#100, #104-#107).

Plausible reason: the wide 64-byte BVH already keeps the tree compact and the triangle buffer is only ~3.3 MB, so the locality gain is smaller than the cost of the extra indirection/build churn, and the bunny's rays hit triangles that are already fairly coherent.

Decision: reverted; the shipped builder fills TriData up front in original triangle order, which is exactly what the current pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp header comment says ("the payload is the triangle index into TriData (which keeps the original triangle order)", read at #94/#281) and what my later note at #284 recorded. TriData in tree / leaf-emission order: tried, measured, and REJECTED — the shipped round-3 code keeps TriData in original triangle order.

What I did: in the wide-node builder I removed the up-front TriData fill and instead appended each triangle's record at leaf-emission time, storing that new slot index in the leaf payload word, so spatially adjacent leaves index adjacent triangle records (history #87-#107; the change compiled after fixing the n==1 degenerate path, #102-#105).

What it measured (same-session interleaved A/B, 3 reps each, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1, scene-default.json 512x512/64spp, tree-order binary vs scratch/wideA = identical wide-node build with random/original TriData order, #112):

So leaf-emission order came out ~2.4% slower on render_ms_best and ~3.6% slower on gpu_ms_best — it lost rather than won, well outside the noise in the wrong direction. Plausible reason: the bunny's rays hit triangles that are already correlated with the OBJ's own ordering (the mesh is roughly spatially coherent as stored), so reindexing by tree order shuffled that locality away without gaining much, since the wide-node traversal already streams the triangle record right after the leaf's bounds are in cache.

Decision: reverted (kept only the wins >= ~3% rule, and this was a regression). No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did NOT give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not (and does not) use it. Evidence: an early leaf2 build measured ~33.5 ms, but that build was buggy — it silently dropped roughly half the triangles, so the speedup was fake. After fixing the bug (all triangles present again; RMSE 0.475902 vs baseline 0.475898, i.e. statistically identical), the honest same-session A/B showed leaf2 at ~49.0/49.9/54.5 ms bests versus the 2-wide-node leaf-1 build at 44.3/45.7/46.4 ms — a clear loss, so I reverted pathtracer/ to wide nodes with one triangle per leaf (scratch/revert_leaf2.py, messages #242-#248). The reason: the bunny is a thin shell, so single-triangle leaves shrink the empty space rays walk through far more than the extra leaf visits cost; merging triangles also merges their bounds, which degrades the tree. Current pathtracer/ is the wide-leaf1 tree (69,450 nodes, depth 16), and the later 4-wide-node experiment also failed to beat it (46.1 vs 47.1 ms best mean, under the 3% keep threshold), so leaf-1 wide2 remains the right choice.

What I measured: after switching to 64-byte wide nodes with inline child bounds, I tried leaf size 2 using the free bmin.w payload slot for a second triangle index. A careful same-session A/B (interleaved runs, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1, scene-default) gave wide+leaf2 ≈ 49.8 ms mean best vs ≈ 49.7 ms for the reference build — a wash — while wide+leaf1 in the same session measured 45.7–45.8 ms. So leaf2 was actually ~8% slower than leaf1, and I reverted it (scratch/revert_leaf2.py) back to single-triangle leaves. Evidence: my log entries and history messages #186 (plan), #242 ("Honest A/B: fixed leaf2 (wide+leaf2) ≈ 49.8 ms mean vs R02 49.7 → WASH ... leaf2 likely LOSES vs wide+leaf1").

Why it loses: the bunny is a thin shell, so shrinking empty space matters more than node count — merged two-triangle bounds make leaf boxes fatter, so rays test more triangles and the extra triangle test also costs. Merged bounds additionally risk changing closest-hit tie behaviour, which the exactness constraint forbids.

For context, the opposite direction did pay off: leaf size 1 was the single biggest GPU win in round 2 (~10%, from ~55 ms to ~50 ms), and wide nodes made single-triangle leaves free (they occupy no node slot at all). Current pathtracer/ therefore uses leaf size 1 with 64-byte wide nodes. (Separate note: the round-3 4-wide-node experiment I just measured is also a wash — ~46.2 vs ~47.1 ms over 4 interleaved reps, inside noise, so it does not clear the 3% bar either.)
